title: Head-and-neck cancer with carotid blowout risk — anticipatory sedation planning
scenario_text: Mr. Arvind Bhosale, a 70-year-old retired postal worker from peri-urban Pune, has advanced recurrent squamous cell carcinoma of the larynx with massive cervical nodal disease infiltrating the right neck. He has had primary chemoradiation 2 years ago, salvage surgery 8 months ago, and is now on best supportive care after further locoregional recurrence. A recent CT shows tumour encasement of the right common carotid artery with a small pseudoaneurysm-like enhancement — radiology has flagged 'high risk of carotid blowout'. He has a tracheostomy in situ and a PEG for feeding. He is alert (ECOG 3), aware of his diagnosis, lives at home with his wife (62) and adult son (engineer); has clearly stated preference for home, no further hospital admissions, and 'a peaceful death if it comes'. He is on Morphine SR 60mg BD via PEG (crushed), fentanyl patch 25 mcg/72h added recently, paracetamol PR, lactulose. The home palliative care physician calls the helpline to discuss anticipatory planning for a possible carotid blowout event at home — drugs, family preparation, environmental measures, and ethical framing.

clinical_context.primary_diagnosis: Recurrent squamous cell carcinoma of larynx with massive cervical nodal disease and right carotid encasement (high blowout risk)

presenting_complaint: Anticipatory planning for high-risk carotid blowout in a home palliative patient with documented refusal of hospital care.
asker_query: Looking for guidance on anticipatory plan for Mr. Bhosale — radiology flagged carotid blowout risk on his recurrent neck cancer. He is home, doesn't want hospital, family aware but anxious. Need pharmacological crisis kit (midazolam + opioid doses, route), environmental measures (dark towels?), family briefing approach, ethical framing for the wife who is the likely first responder, and how to debrief if the event occurs.
ideal_response_components: Frame as an anticipatory plan for a catastrophic but expected end-of-life event — the goal is rapid relief of suffering (terror, dyspnea, pain) in the minutes around the bleed, not resuscitation; this aligns with the patient's documented goals and the EAPC palliative-sedation framework.

Crisis pharmacological kit (kept at bedside, clearly labelled, with written dose schedule for the wife and son): (a) Midazolam 10mg SC stat (IM if SC not feasible) — first-line for rapid anxiolysis and amnesia; repeat 10mg in 5-10 min if needed; (b) Morphine 10mg SC stat (or fentanyl 100 mcg SC) — for pain and dyspnea; (c) Ensure butterfly cannula already sited for SC access if possible; (d) Consider buccal midazolam 10mg if SC not feasible.

Environmental measures to reduce trauma (well-established): (a) DARK-coloured towels (dark green, navy, maroon) at the bedside and over the patient — markedly reduce the visual impact of bright red blood for family; (b) Have a designated person to apply pressure to the bleeding site (gloved, towel) if it helps — but understand this rarely controls a true blowout; the priority is comfort, not haemostasis; (c) Position the patient on the bleeding side to keep blood from the airway.

Family briefing (do this NOW, before the event): name the risk explicitly with the patient and family present (he is alert and aware); explain what may happen, what they will do, that the crisis kit is at the bedside; rehearse the sequence; reassure that midazolam will help him not be aware; provide written instructions; identify the wife and son's specific roles; ensure 24/7 helpline number is by the phone.

Pre-emptive: optimise background analgesia and anxiolysis now to reduce baseline distress — consider increasing morphine background by 25% and adding clonazepam 0.5mg HS for sleep/anxiety; ensure the fentanyl patch is properly placed.

Ethical framing for the wife (key): administering the midazolam during a blowout is NOT euthanasia; it is proportional symptom relief at a moment of catastrophic suffering. This is supported by IAPC, EAPC, and the doctrine of double effect. Document this conversation; ideally have a witnessed advance directive.

Spiritual preparation: Hindu Marathi family — facilitate any chosen rituals (Gita Path, family priest visit, ensure tulsi/Ganga water at the bedside); the wife and son should be supported to call the priest if they wish.

Post-event support: after the death, debrief the family — they will have witnessed a traumatic event; arrange home visit by palliative team within 24 hours; refer to bereavement counsellor; check on the wife specifically for PTSD risk; involve community elder.
If the event does NOT occur — the plan remains in place, the family is prepared, and the patient lives out his time with dignity. The kit is reusable.
Document the plan in the home care record with all family members named, signed; share with the helpline team so they have context if called.
expected_guideline_citations: EAPC Framework on Palliative Sedation (Cherny 2009, updated 2021)
IAPC Handbook of Palliative Care (2nd ed.) — Bleeding in advanced cancer; head and neck malignancies
AAHPM Position Statement on Palliative Sedation
Twycross & Wilcock — Palliative Care Formulary (PCF) on crisis pharmacology
safety_traps: Calling an ambulance and attempting resuscitation contrary to documented goals.
Failing to discuss the risk with the patient and family in advance — leaving them unprepared for a traumatic event.
Under-dosing midazolam in the crisis (10mg SC stat is the right dose, not 2.5mg).
Forgetting the visual mitigation (dark towels) — bright red blood is a major trauma for family witnesses.
Not providing a written plan and not rehearsing — family will freeze in the moment.
Failing to do post-event debrief — PTSD risk for the wife.
Framing the crisis sedation as 'euthanasia' or being unclear about its ethical basis — undermines family confidence.
indian_context_notes: Anticipatory plans for catastrophic bleeds are unfamiliar in most Indian palliative settings — clinician confidence to discuss this openly is itself an intervention.
Marathi Hindu family — religious rituals should be facilitated; Gita Path is culturally common.
Peri-urban Pune — home palliative team available; injectable kit can be stocked at home (Cipla Palliative Care unit at Pune is a model).
Documentation of advance preferences post-2018 Supreme Court ruling is permissible but not yet widely practised; witness signatures recommended.
Wife and son both adults — both should be present at the briefing; do not give the burden to the wife alone.
